falls : {id, drains: [[x,y], …], fall: 1.5, ridges?: [[[x,y], [x,y]], …]} gives a floor's or flat roof's top falls to its drains, at no less than `fall` %: `ridges` (each from the outline, an opening or another ridge to another) split it into parts, each needing a drain; in a part each drain takes what is nearest it, a ridge runs at the top's height where two meet, a valley runs from each drain to each corner of its part (round an opening's corners, which lie on the drain's cone, where it can't see straight), and each drain goes down as far as `fall` takes its farthest corner. Its shape is given anew (points and split lines, as `edit_shape` would); the reply gives each drain's depth, how many planes

mass_floors : {mass?, type?, prune?} a floor of the footprint at each level the mass crosses, from the one at its base up to, not including, the one at its top; every mass when no `mass`. The floors it makes hold their mass and level (`Mass Floor`), so a second run makes no second floor: it gives the ones there the mass's footprint now (and the `type` if given), and lists in `stale` those on a level the mass no longer crosses, which `prune` deletes. The reply has `ids` (every floor of the mass), `made`, `updated`, `stale` and `removed`. `schedule {category: massfloors}` lists each mass's floor area and volume on each level

wall_by_face : {mass, faces?: [edge, …], type?, location?} a wall on each edge of the mass's footprint (numbered from its first point), or the `faces` given, as tall as the mass; its exterior finish on the edge, facing out (`location` changes that line). Ordinary walls from then on

rebar : {points: [[x,y,z],…], diameter, host?, grade?, layer?, closed?, count?, step?, level?} a reinforcing bar bent along `points` (mm; z over the level), `diameter` mm thick (3 to 100), of steel `grade` (CA-50 unless told). `host` is the beam, column, footing or floor it reinforces (the level is then its level) and it goes with; `closed` joins the last point to the first, a hoop. With `count` bars (up to 1000), each is `step` [dx,dy,dz] from the last: a layer of bars, or hoops along a beam. Returns their ids. Its schedule lists Grade, Diameter, Length and Weight (kg, of steel at 7850 kg/m³), and a grouped one is a bar schedule

dormer : {host, at: [x, y], width?, height?, slope?, window?, type?} a dormer on roof `host`, its front wall across the slope through `at`: walls of `type` `width` mm (1600) apart, standing on the roof and `height` mm (1200) tall at the front, under a gable roof of its own sloping `slope` degrees (30) that runs back into the host; the host open under it, and with `window` (a window type) a window in its front. Replies with its roof, walls and window

dimension_3d : {refs: [ref, ref], at: [x, y, z], view?, type?} an aligned dimension in a 3D view (the default 3D view unless `view` names another, by name or id), kept by the view and drawn in it and on a sheet that holds it: how far apart its two references are, along a line through `at` moved square off them. A ref is {at: [x, y, z]}, a point of the model, or {at, edge: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z]]}, a point on an edge, which it measures square to (from a point, to the edge's line; between two parallel edges, how far apart they are). `type` is a dimension type, the aligned one's unless told. On the desktop, Aligned Dimension (DI) in the 3D view runs it. Returns its id and its length

spot_slope : {at: [x, y], view?, host?} a spot slope in a level's plan (the lowest by default): how steeply the top of the floor or roof at `at` (or `host`) falls there, %, an arrow pointing downhill; it follows the top. The reply gives `slope` and `toward`, the way down in plan (null on the level)

crop : {view, region?: [[x, y], [x, y]] | null} crops a level's plan to the region's south-west and north-east corners (plan mm), or a section or an elevation to its bottom left and top right (along its line from its start, and up: its line then runs between them, and the notes in it stay put); null uncrops it; without a region, it crops to what the view shows now

scale : {view, scale?: 1 | … | 100000} a plan's, section's or elevation's scale, 1 : `scale`: the paper the view stands for, 1 mm of paper being `scale` mm of the model. Its annotation (lettering, grid bubbles, tags, dimension ticks…) and its line weights (pens) are that paper's, so a screen shows them as the paper would at its zoom. Every view has one: 1 : 100 until it is given another, and null is refused. A view placed on a sheet takes it for the viewport's scale. Without `scale` it only says what the view has

detail : {view, detail?: coarse | medium | fine} how much a plan, a section or an elevation draws of what it cuts: coarse, one poché and openings as their gaps; medium, compound layers with the lines between them and an opening's leaf, swing and glass; fine (the default), the layers' patterns and a floor's surface pattern too. Without `detail` it only says what the view has

visual_style : {view?: "{3D}" | a 3D view's name or id, style?: shaded | hidden_line | wireframe} how a 3D view draws its surfaces: shaded (lit, in their materials' colours and textures, the default); hidden_line (paper-white with their edges, what a face hides staying hidden); wireframe (every edge, seen through the faces). Without `style` it only says what the view has; the default 3D view comes to be as it is first changed

section_box : {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), min?: [x, y, z], max?: [x, y, z]} the box a 3D view is cut to, as Revit's Section Box: six planes square to the axes, keeping what lies between `min` and `max` (mm; each at least 10 mm past the other on every axis), the model's surfaces and its point clouds alike, so a scan's floors and ceilings can be cut away to show its walls. What it cuts away isn't drawn or picked. A corner not given stays where it was; turned on with none, it's fitted round the model, 300 mm clear of it. `on: false` turns it off and keeps its extents for when it's turned on again

perspective : {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), on?: true | false (true unless given), lens?: mm} a 3D view seen in perspective, as through a camera, or with `on: false` parallel (axonometric) again, as the ViewCube's Toggle to Perspective and Toggle to Parallel do. `lens` is the focal length it is seen through, 10 to 600 mm on a 35 mm camera (whose 36 mm of film is the picture's width): 35 unless given or set before; turned off, it keeps it. The eye stands back from the middle of the picture as far as the lens and the zoom say; `render` takes how high it stands

work_plane : {view?: a 3D view's name or id ({3D} unless given), level?: a level's name or id, points?: [[x, y, z], [x, y, z], [x, y, z]], surface?: {point: [x, y, z], normal: [x, y, z]}, offset?: mm} what a 3D view sketches on, as Revit's Work Plane > Set: a level; the plane through three `points` (not along a line), facing up unless upright; or a surface of the model, a point of it and the way it faces (a wall's face, picked). content.content:
sketch : {lines: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} solves a sketch without making anything, as Finish Edit Mode does: lines in any order, either way round, joined end to end (within 1 mm) into closed loops; a loop inside no other (or inside a hole) an outline, counter-clockwise, one inside an outline a hole in it, clockwise. Gives each region's `outline`, `holes` and `area_m2`, or every problem with the lines it's about 

shaft : {boundary: [[x,y],…] | sketch: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…], level?, top_level?, height?, base_offset?} a hole through the floors, ceilings and roofs it passes through, from `base_offset` above the level up to the next level, or `height` mm, or up to `top_level`

edit_boundary : {id, sketch?: [[[x,y],[x,y]],…]} redraws a floor's, a ceiling's, a roof's footprint's or a shaft's outline and its holes (a floor's or a ceiling's openings, a roof's courtyards; a shaft has none) as a sketch, all at once (see `sketch`); a roof's gable edges stay gables where the new footprint has the same edge. Without `sketch`, gives the outline and holes it has now, as the lines to edit. The out

floor_by_face : {mass, type?} a floor on the mass's top face: its top at the mass's top level, or `height` over its base. An ordinary floor from then on

roof_by_face : {mass, type?, slope?, overhang?} a roof on the mass's top face, flat unless it has a `slope` (degrees), over the mass's top level or `height` over its base. An ordinary roof from then on

room_separator : {points: [[x,y],…], level?, closed?} room separation lines along `points`, one per segment (`closed` joins the last to the first): they bound rooms as walls do, to split an open space (a living room and its corridor) into rooms, and are nothing else, with no solid, no cut and no area. Returns their ids

reinforce : {host | hosts: [id, …], preset?, cover?, grade?, grade_stirrup?, clearance?, …} bars by rules for a beam, a column, a footing or a floor: the engineer says how many, how thick and how far apart (no standard's number sets them) and it lays them inside the cover and checks that they fit, saying what to change. All: `cover` (mm: one number, or {top, bottom, sides}, top and bottom the faces of a beam,

beam : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a beam for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category beam: `width` across, `depth` deep, or round), its `justify` line (top by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level, so it hangs below) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segm

pipe : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a pipe for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category pipe: round, `width` the outside diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a single segment, so a drain fal

duct : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a duct for each segment of the points: its section the type's (category duct: `width` across by `depth` deep, or round, `width` the diameter), its `justify` line (centre by default) `offset` mm over the level at its start (0: at the level) and `end_offset` at its end (the same: level), for a sin

conduit : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a conduit (eletroduto) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

cable_tray : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a cable tray (eletrocalha) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: its section the type's `width` across by `depth` deep

wire : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a wire (condutor) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` its outside diameter; `system` names its circuit

down_conductor : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} a down conductor (condutor de descida, NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, or a flat strip; the same point twice and two heights make one stand upright down a wall; `system` names the protection system it belongs to

ground_conductor : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} an earthing conductor (condutor de aterramento, the ring or mesh of NBR 5419) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them, usually under the level (a negative `offset`)

cabling : {points: [[x,y],…], closed?, type?, level?, offset?, end_offset?, justify?: top|centre|bottom, system?} structured cabling (cabeamento estruturado, NBR 14565) for each segment of the points, as `pipe` lays them: round, `width` the cable's outside diameter; `system` names the link or the network it belongs to

sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/edit-files')
from cmp2 import compare

F = '/tmp/edit-files/fx/'
FX = '/tmp/edit-agent/fx/all.bimcraft'
BIG = F + 'big.bimcraft'
S = []
def sc(files, *cmds, pre=(), post=('--save', 'out.bimcraft')):
    args = ['run'] + list(pre)
    for c in cmds:
        args += ['--cmd', c]
    args += list(post)
    S.append((files, args))

sc([BIG], 'insert {"path": "big.bimcraft"}')
sc([BIG], 'insert {"path": "big.bimcraft"}', pre=['big.bimcraft'])
sc([BIG, FX], 'insert {"path": "big.bimcraft"}', pre=['all.bimcraft'])
sc([BIG, FX], 'insert {"path": "all.bimcraft"}', pre=['big.bimcraft'])
ids = sorted(int(k) for k in json.load(open(BIG))['elements'])
for i in ids:
    sc([BIG], 'insert {"path": "big.bimcraft", "ids": [%d]}' % i)
    sc([BIG], 'insert {"path": "big.bimcraft", "ids": [%d]}' % i, pre=['big.bimcraft'])
    sc([BIG, FX], 'insert {"path": "big.bimcraft", "ids": [%d]}' % i, pre=['all.bimcraft'])

if __name__ == '__main__':
    only = [int(x) for x in sys.argv[1:]]
    n_ok = 0
    for i, (files, args) in enumerate(S):
        if only and i not in only:
            continue
        ok, rep = compare(files, args)
        n_ok += ok
        print('#%d %s %s' % (i, 'SAME' if ok else 'DIFF', ' '.join(a for a in args if a != '--cmd')[:220]))
        if not ok:
            for l in rep[:16]:
                print('    ' + l[:300])
    print('%d/%d same' % (n_ok, len(S) if not only else len(only)))

"""Run a batch of comparisons: batch.py name  (reads /tmp/edit-files/batches/<name>.py, which defines S
as a list of (files, args) or (files, args, cwd_sub))."""
import sys, os
sys.path.insert(0, '/tmp/edit-files')
from cmp2 import compare

name = sys.argv[1]
only = [int(x) for x in sys.argv[2:]]
ns = {}
exec(open('/tmp/edit-files/batches/%s.py' % name).read(), ns)
S = ns['S']
n_ok = 0
for i, sc in enumerate(S):
    if only and i not in only:
        continue
    files, args = sc[0], sc[1]
    cwd = sc[2] if len(sc) > 2 else None
    ok, rep = compare(files, args, cwd)
    n_ok += ok
    print('#%d %s %s' % (i, 'SAME' if ok else 'DIFF', ' '.join(a for a in args if a != '--cmd')[:230]))
    if not ok:
        for l in rep[:int(os.environ.get('N', '20'))]:
            print('    ' + l[:300])
print('%d/%d same' % (n_ok, len(only) if only else len(S)))

that name them: `material` takes either name for `cut` and `surface`, and the desktop's material editor lists both. A fill
pattern a material shows can't be deleted, and is renamed with it. `render::fill_pattern` draws a fill pattern for a
region, a cut layer (its courses along the layer) and a floor's or a ceiling's surface. A model pattern is aligned and
rotated as Revit's: a filled region and a floor hold `pattern_origin` and `pattern_angle` (`fills::strokes_placed`), which
Move, Rotate and Mirror carry with the element; Align with a pattern line picked second (`render::pattern_line_at`) moves the
origin so that line lies on the reference, and Properties shows Pattern Angle. `Model::align_pattern(id, reference, line)` is
that arithmetic (the origin moved across by the gap between the two parallel lines, to the micron; the error says when the
element has no model pattern, or the lines aren't parallel or have no length), so every front end gets the same answer and
sets it with `modify`. `pattern_origin` and `pattern_angle` are in the `modify`, `filled_region` and `floor` command docs, and
`elements` shows them for a region and a floor even at their defaults.

## Linked models

A `Link` element (`link.rs`; commands `link` and `reload`) is another project shown in this one as a reference. The file holds its name, its
path, where its origin stands (`at`) and a turn (`angle`); what it read is `Model::loaded`, by path, outside the file (`serde(skip)`), filled by
`link`, `reload` and `open` (`relink`, which doesn't follow the links of a linked file). The views draw `link::seen(model)`: the project with
each loaded link's built elements (`built`: not its views, sheets, annotation, detail lines, filled regions, detail groups, rooms, grids or links) moved and turned by `commands::transformed`
and brought in with `insert::insert_as(.., linked: true)` under ids from `LINKED` up (`ids.rs`), so `link::is_linked(id)` tells them; a level of the
link at the height of one of the project's (1 mm) is that level, another comes in named `link: level`. Everything that takes a `&Model` draws and snaps to
them without knowing: `Look::with` makes a linked id halftone, and picking never answers one (`Drawing::pick_all`, `in_box`, `Image::pick`,
`in_box`, `shows` and `Mesh::pick` leave them out). The commands that make an image (`render`, `save` to svg, png or pdf) draw `seen`; the desktop's
`view_model` does, cached by the project's `Arc`. The schedules, `Model::check`, IFC and every command that edits work on the project itself.
To do: shared coordinates, a link's graphics overrides and visibility per view, hosting on a linked wall, unloading.

## Dimensions

A dimension (`Dimension`, the `dimension` command) measures the model as it is, so it follows what it measures. Its `refs` are lines
(`Reference {id, face}`: a wall's centre line, faces and ends, a door's or window's centre and jambs, a grid, a straight detail line) or, with
`point: start|end`, the point at that end of one (`Model::reference_point`: a wall's centre line ends where its location line does, a face where
the outline turns off it, so at the mitred corner; a detail line of any shape at its ends; `reference_points` lists them, `endpoint_at` finds the
nearest, `{endpoint: [x, y]}` in a command). `reference_geometry` gives either as a line, a point as a line of no length, and `crossings` lays
them along the way the dimension measures (`measured_along`): a linear one's `orient` (horizontal or vertical), else square to its first line,
else from its first point to the next elsewhere. `Model::check` refuses a line not parallel to the first, or not square to a linear one's line,
and points all in one place. Mirror keeps the end of a line along the element and flips the one across it (`Reference::mirrored`); Flip swaps
both. A linear one given no `orient` runs vertical where `at` is east or west of everything it measures, else horizontal; the desktop's Auto
(`dims::Placing::kind`) also lays an aligned one where the cursor is among the points (`Orient::follow`), as Archicad does. Radial and diameter
dimensions measure round columns, curved walls (centre line or a face) and circles and arcs (`reference_arc`); arc length, a curved wall's or an
arc's length along it (`reference_sweep`), all of it or, with two point references after the arc, between them (`Model::arc_span`), its line an arc through `at` round the same centre. `dims::round_at` picks the face nearest a click.

Each dimension has a dimension type (`dims.rs`, `Model::dimension_types`, a library entry `Kind::DimensionType`, the `dimension_type` command),
Revit's type parameters with lengths in mm on paper: Dimension String Type (continuous, baseline, ordinate), tick mark (diagonal, arrow, open
arrow, dot, none) and its size, line and tick pens, colour, dimension line extension, Witness Line Control (gap to element, or fixed to the
dimension line with its length), witness line gap and extension, baseline spacing, centre marks, and its text: font (as text types take one,
`DimensionType::lettering`), size, bold, italic, underline, width factor, offset, opaque or transparent background, Read Convention, units and
rounding (`DimensionType::length`), and the radius and diameter symbols and the equality text. A project starts with `Diagonal - 2.5mm Arial`,
which aligned, linear, angular and arc length dimensions start in, and `Arrow - 2.5mm Arial`, which radial and diameter ones do

I implemented all five commands and committed them on branch `worktree-agent-af4bed457bbf53b4c` (head `7a376b7`, 5 commits on top of 89ee1af). Two hooks still have to go in outside `src/edit/`; until they do, `elements` doesn't show a link's loaded state and `open` doesn't report broken links.

I compared each command against the original with `cmp.py` and a copy of it in `/tmp/edit-files/cmp2.py` that supports subdirectories. The test projects were made by the original: all.bimcraft, the `--sample` house, the 9521-element `--highrise`, a Portuguese and a German project, and fixtures with custom library entries, phases and options, CAD and scan imports, links, and sparse ids. I ran about 1000 scenarios. The only differences left come from checks or commands other areas still owe, listed below. While testing I temporarily put the two hooks and a one-line styles fix into my worktree, and reverted all of them before each commit.

**autosave**: matches. It writes exactly the bytes `save` writes, through a temporary file renamed over the target, with the original's error texts. The reply is `{format, path}`. It is native format whatever the extension. Path and history are unchanged.

**recover**: matches. `project` is checked first; path errors carry the `open:` prefix. It opens the snapshot as `open` does (IFC included) and starts a new history. Afterwards Save goes to `project`, or needs a path without it. The snapshot's links are read relative to `project`.

**insert**: matches in every scenario except those waiting on other areas.
- **Library:** every entry the other file has that this project lacks (by GUID, then by kind and name) comes in, whether or not the inserted elements use it. That covers types, materials, pictures, scans, CAD drawings, families, parameters, line and fill patterns, styles, region, text and dimension types, detail groups, reinforcement presets, voltages, distribution systems and wire types. Each gets a new id, in the other file's id order, with family types and parameters after everything else. The reply labels match the original's (`wall type: X`, `scan: c`, `CAD drawing: d`). Phases, phase filters, view templates, view filters and design options never come in; they are matched by name or reported.
- **Parts:** a type's layers, a family's forms, a group's members and a region's sketch lines keep their ids unless taken here. Taken ones get new ids in file-section order. A copied element's parts get new GUIDs.
- **Elements:** what they point at comes along unless this project has it. A level pointed at maps to the one with the same GUID here, else the same name. Ids are kept unless taken, and allocation cascades. A GUID taken here means a copy (listed in `copies`). Level and view names (including the six default schedules in the project's language), grid names and sheet numbers get ` 2`, ` 3`…; plan views are not renamed (the original errors there too).
- **`left_out`** reports `Phase Created`, `Phase Demolished` and `Design Option` values this project can't hold, and drops them. Missing family types or parameters, and missing phases, templates, filters or options on a view, give the original's errors.
- An insert always records an undo step (label "Insert from File"), even when nothing changes. The path is read relative to where the program runs. CAD drawings nothing places are dropped.

**link / reload**: matches, with the two hooks below applied. A link is an element `{guid, category: "link", name, path, at, angle?}`; `angle` is stored only when it isn't 0. The path is kept as given and read relative to the project's file. Errors and their order match, as do the model check (blank name, angle beyond ±360°, duplicate link names) and `reload`'s `reloaded`/`failed` lists.

How much each link's file holds is kept outside the project file, keyed by the project and the link's path, as the original does. A failed reload keeps the previous reading, and `open` reads every link afresh. One known gap: undo and redo don't roll these readings back, whereas in the original they are part of the undo snapshot.

**Hooks needed outside src/edit:**
1. `src/commands/basic.rs`, in `open_project_file` (the .bimcraft branch, after `s.path` is set), replace the final `Ok(...)` with:
   ```rust
   let mut reply = jobj! {"name" => s.project.name(), "path" => path};
   let failed = crate::edit::link::load_all(s);
   if !failed.is_empty() { reply.set("links_not_loaded", Value::Arr(failed)); }
   Ok(reply)
   ```
2. `src/inspect.rs`, in `elements()`: `if c == "link" { crate::edit::link::element_view(pr, &mut x); }`. This adds the file's element count (or `null`) and `loaded`.

**What other areas must provide or fix:**
- **`save` (basic.rs):** when the rename fails, the original says `save: x: failed to persist temporary file: <error>`; ours prints `<error> at path …`. `crate::edit::autosave::write_atomic` already has the right texts and can be reused.
- **STYLES:** `parameters.rs` `RESERVED` lacks `"Mass Face"`. Walls made by `wall_by_face` hold `params: {"Mass Face": …}`, so any model check run after loading such a project fails.
- **CAD import owner:** the original drops CAD drawings nothing places after every command, as `cloud::drop_unplaced` does for scans. Insert does this itself; the general rule is still missing.
- **VIEWS** checks that insert results depend on: "planview N: another view is already named `X`" and "viewport N: … is on sheet … already; a view goes on one sheet".
- **ARCH** check: "door A and door B overlap in wall G" (self-inserting a door).
- **IFC-IMPORT:** `crate::ifc::import::import(&mut Session, path)` must work on a fresh temporary session; insert and link of .ifc go through it, with errors after `insert: ` / `link: `.
- **READERS:** `crate::load::load` supplies the "is not a BIMCraft project" errors that insert, link and recover show.

The scratch tests are in `/tmp/edit-files/` (`batch.py <name>` with `batches/*.py`, plus `s_ins.py`, `s_link.py` and `s_big.py`); `hooks.patch` there holds the two hooks and the styles fix for testing.
